analysis.title: The volatility trap Wall Street is facing: a massive two-way risk
key_insights: SPX closed at its lowest level since May. VIX is overshooting the move in SPX even though the last three sessions were an orderly grind lower rather than outright panic in spot.
VIX is at 25 and VVIX at 121, so uncertainty about the path of VIX itself remains elevated.
VXN rose less than VIX in the latest session, but the gap between the two remains very wide. Volatility is elevated across the board, with stress particularly pronounced in tech.
Skew has been rising since early October. Downside protection stays well bid in relative volatility terms, with little sign of the crowd monetizing hedges despite the sell-off.
Nomura estimates aggregate SPX dealer gamma at about negative $7.3bn, near the bottom of its historical range. Dealer hedging can amplify moves in either direction.
Nomura's McElligott sees the VIX floor shifting higher, but limited positioning fuel for a volatility shock above 30 without a much deeper equity selloff.

Nomura estimates systematic equity strategies sold $116bn over the past two weeks, taking aggregate exposure to the 10th percentile. Prime brokerage net leverage is at zero or low single digits, and Mag7 call skew is at the 12th percentile.
McElligott sees potential for a 'buyers are higher' squeeze if volatility starts to cool, because a large amount of risk has already been removed.

Nomura's model shows a further 5% equity decline could trigger about $81.8bn of mechanical selling from options dealers, leveraged ETFs and volatility-control strategies. A 5% rally would imply about $66.1bn of buying.
risk_factors: Negative dealer gamma amplifies moves in either direction.
Mechanical flows from dealers, leveraged ETFs and vol-control funds of $66-82bn on a 5% move either way.
A volatility cooldown could trigger a squeeze higher as underexposed systematic and discretionary investors re-buy.
A deeper equity selloff is needed for VIX to spike above 30, but could force further systematic selling.
